summary: Top Traders Unplugged Ep.364: Moritz and Niels discuss 2025 trend-following (commodity-led, April losses), portfolio construction via independent markets, execution/delayed exits, simple entry rules and dynamic position sizing trade-offs. They summarize a Don Capital paper (caption spelling) showing trend ranks best on drawdown/vol and crisis protection, and explain why alternative-fund vol has fallen.

coverage.note: tennis/cycling chat, long-end bond yields and fiscal concern
trend-following year to date, commodity-led returns, Liberation Day losses
coffee, bond model disagreement, index performance, diversification intro
venue differences (COMEX vs LME copper), slippage, delayed exits
next-day execution, anecdote, avoiding stop hunts, simplicity
derivative-free indicators, importance of entry, hit rate

paper results: Sharpe, drawdown/vol, correlation, portfolio

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: UK bonds, 30-year bonds, hit the highest yield in 27 years, even higher than the so-called list truss moment
claims.claim: UK 30-year gilt yields hit a 27-year high and US yields neared 5% while economies were soft, which Niels reads as a possible 2022-like environment that favors trend following.
claims.indicator: UK 30y gilt yield, US 30y yield, Bund 30y

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: there is a concern that the you know fiscal positions of these countries the countries we live in um they're no longer strong
claims.claim: Long-end yields are rising (curve steepening) because investors demand more yield to fund weak fiscal positions, with gold sniffing this out.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: livestock live cattle is quite a fantastic trend for a couple of years now
claims.claim: Longer-term trends have re-established in equities, livestock and gold, while the financial sectors (bonds in a huge range, equities with sharp politically driven corrections, currencies) have been hard for trend followers.
claims.conditions: trends in commodities carried 2025 while financials whipsawed

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: it's really been a year of the commodities they are driving our returns
claims.claim: This year's trend-following returns come from long livestock (lean hogs, live and feeder cattle) and precious metals (platinum, silver, gold), with long cocoa still held.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: Then it takes a long while to get back in if you get back in.
claims.claim: Losses in currencies, equities and bonds came from the April 2025 Liberation Day reversals: slow long-term models were stopped out and then re-enter only after a long delay.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: our systems determine them to be still trading rangebound
claims.claim: Several bond markets are rangebound by the system's rules, so it holds no position there and is underexposed to fixed income.
claims.testable: yes: no signal means no position

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: we've had this strong bull market in coffee which was great for us and then moved down now it's moving up again so we kind of like reversed going back in
claims.claim: Coffee gave large gains in its bull run then whipsaw, an example of trend reversals costing profits but the system re-entering.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: a little bit of a um um quote unquote disagreement among managers right now or the models uh as to whether you should be fully long or fully short or somewhere in between
claims.claim: Trend models disagree on bonds (daily returns of CTA funds diverge with bond moves), which supports blending managers by speed and time frame.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: it's flat so far this September but it is down 6.46% for the year
claims.claim: SG CTA -2.7%, Trend index -7.25% and Short-Term Traders -6.46% YTD, versus MSCI World +13.6%, S&P 500 +10.6% and US Agg +5%.
claims.indicator: SG CTA, SG Trend, SG Short-Term Traders indices

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: we're building a portfolio of these constituents where ideally there's just nothing that links between them
claims.claim: Portfolio construction goal: as many truly independent return streams as possible (cocoa vs S&P, sugar vs OJ, California carbon vs 10-year), not a target market count.
claims.testable: yes: test diversification benefit by market set

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: So, if we can apply it to as many independent markets and return streams as we possibly can, then in expectation our um return stream will be improving.
claims.claim: Casino analogy: a small trend edge applied across many independent bets raises expected risk-adjusted return.
claims.conditions: needs the edge to be real and bets independent

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: which is why we've made the decision to limit the size of our firm or our fund to 500 million
claims.claim: Small diversifying markets (Chinese futures, canola, lumber, livestock, carbon) cannot absorb big capital, so capacity is capped around $500 million to keep a meaningful footprint.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: the largest and the most liquid market with screen liquidity
claims.claim: EU carbon allowances (EUA) on ICE trade with screen liquidity and about a cent or two bid-offer, so they are efficient to trade as futures.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: So California is absolutely uncorrelated um to EUAs and the EUAS are uncorrelated to the Reggie market which is the east coast of the US.
claims.claim: Regional carbon markets (California, EU, RGGI) are mutually uncorrelated while EUA and UKA moved together after relinking talk, so each adds diversification.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: you're probably getting a better execution than, you know, just going um going on screen
claims.claim: Brokered futures markets (CCAs, South African grains) cost a penny more but may give better execution than hitting screen quotes, so they are not 'crappy' markets.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: the Comx copper or the CME copper market in the US and the LME copper market, they tend to be very highly and persistently correlated and now they've decoupled
claims.claim: Tariff news decoupled COMEX and LME copper, so the same commodity can behave differently by venue.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: the delivery mechanics um the warehouse locations what can be delivered from where they they're different
claims.claim: London vs New York sugar, coffee and cocoa differ in delivery and grade, so they can diverge; the manager trades all of them and splits risk.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: whether you have a resting stop in the order book
claims.claim: A COMEX copper long exited around 4.6 after a tariff gap (theoretical exit north of 5.17) because there are no resting stops and exits are delayed.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: we find that there's actually an improvement to have these um delayed exits
claims.claim: Across all systems and markets, delayed exits (next-day execution) give slightly better returns than stop orders.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: So we get a signal to take a position based on the last available settlement price and then we would implement that signal um usually on the next day settlement.
claims.claim: Signals use the last settlement and trade the next day settlement, with no stop orders, to avoid being picked off.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: delaying your actual execution by a whole week was a better
claims.claim: A manager found in 2014 that delaying execution by a whole week gave better overall returns than reacting immediately.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: We just don't want any of these um like oneoff random price events to kick us out of a position and um interfere with our models.
claims.claim: Flash spikes (e.g. South African rand) can trigger resting stops; delayed exits avoid being kicked out by one-off glitches.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: one of the ways to create robustness and increase resilience is to use relatively simple rules
claims.claim: Simple rules (Occam's razor) are more robust; extra filters and parameters mainly improve backtests, not future returns.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: is the price today higher than the price 100 days ago
claims.claim: Entries use derivative-free indicators (price vs price N days ago, new 200-day high), avoiding moving averages though those also work.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: for a long-term trend following system, it doesn't move the needle that much
claims.claim: The entry signal is both most and least important: whether MA, breakout, today or three days later matters little for a long-term trend system.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: like you know 70% of our trades are losing trades only 30% of them are winning trades
claims.claim: About 70% of trades lose and 30% win, so the entry signal quality is weak and profit comes from outliers.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: we're just ruthless in keeping these losses small
claims.claim: Profit comes from keeping losses small via initial position size, stop placement and exit on give-back, not from entries.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: Keeping losses small and letting these profits run uh appropriately sizing trades.
claims.claim: Key drivers of trend success, in order: diversification across independent markets, small losses and letting profits run, and sizing.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: You can actually use a random entry methodology um and if you randomly enter the market and you have a rule to keep losses small and let profits run you end up making money.
claims.claim: A random entry plus cut-losses and let-winners-run rules makes money (Tom Basso); entries on 100/200-day highs improve on random entry.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: the volatility drag really becomes such a big break where it's very difficult to recover from the from the draw down
claims.claim: Keeping losses small avoids volatility drag that makes drawdowns hard to recover from.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: let's just distinguish that there is kind of like this volatility based or volatility and correlation based dynamic position sizing which some funds are using
claims.claim: Dynamic position sizing has two forms: vol/correlation-based (vol targeting) and risk/heat-based (loss if all stops hit); the firm uses neither except initial sizing.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: They create a more steady return stream.
claims.claim: Vol targeting gives smoother returns and fewer big losses but 'something has to give'.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: The most important one is the initial trade sizing.
claims.claim: Initial trade sizing is the most important risk control; later size changes tend to be profit-taking trades.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: these trades become kind of like mean reversion trades where you go on and off and on and off
claims.claim: Frequent vol-based resizing turns a trend system into mean reversion, adds commissions and bid-offer costs, and cuts the right-tail outliers (gold, livestock this year) that make the year.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: you would now also be reducing your gold position in a long-term uptrend um because of that calculation
claims.claim: Risk-based DPS would trim a long gold position as the price moves away from its exit level, giving back asymmetry; the trade-off is smoother returns and lower drawdowns vs fewer outlier years.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: what you want is really that punchiness
claims.claim: Moritz argues for 'punchy', lopsided returns in stress events, accepting larger give-back potential.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: but what I do like about the the the different approach is when you blend them so to speak you actually diversify the investment process
claims.claim: Blending managers with different position-sizing approaches diversifies the process even when long-term correlation is high.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: we as investors we just do not care whether you DPS or you do not DPS at the end of the day
claims.claim: Some investors (family offices) care only about net performance, while institutions want process detail.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: more diversified programs will generally lose more than less diversified programs
claims.claim: TransTrend argued that in a large correlated shock like the April 2025 tariffs, more diversified programs lose more, since more markets hold positions that are hit together.
claims.indicator: number of markets and shock losses
claims.testable: yes: loss on shock days vs market count

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: and simply because of the fact that you have more markets on will probably make you experience a larger loss on that day.
claims.claim: In big events correlated behavior means more markets with positions give a larger loss; the firm does not force a position in every market.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: comparing the universe of alternative investments to see well what if you could have to pick one maybe two what would be called kind of the most valuable uh alternative investment you could find
claims.claim: Don Capital paper (caption spelling) compares 14 hedge fund strategies and whether leverage or vol changes their value, using the Barclay CTA index back to 1987.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: the rolling three-year analyze volatility of managers is not 20 25% anymore. it's sub 5%.
claims.claim: Rolling three-year annualized volatility of the Barclay CTA index fell from 20-25% to below 5%, due to institutionalization and asset gathering.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: The sharp ratio doesn't make trend following look very good.
claims.claim: Over 25 years of SG Trend data, Sharpe is middling for trend following.
claims.indicator: Sharpe ratio vs other HF strategies

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: trend following comes out uh on top of all of these strategies including by the way the S&P 500
claims.claim: Max drawdown relative to volatility is better for trend following than for all other strategies, including the S&P 500 and world government bonds.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: trend following starts to to pick up a few places to say the least
claims.claim: On correlation, convexity and skew (timing of returns) trend following ranks much better than on Sharpe.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: sharp was never invented to use as on single line items it's a portfolio tool
claims.claim: Sharpe is a portfolio measure: a 20% allocation (50/30/20) of trend raises returns a lot and, with leverage, improves drawdowns though Sharpe is a bit lower.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: if we objectively say a crisis in equity markets is more than 20 25% or more uh draw down in the S&P 500
claims.claim: Four equity crises since 2000 (S&P drawdown above 20-25%): trend following cut portfolio drawdown more than any other strategy.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: Volatility is also opportunity uh to get into very interesting and potentially lucrative trades.
claims.claim: Volatility is not risk for trend followers; it creates opportunity, and hedge fund realized vol has dropped to about half of previous levels.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: if you lower your your volatility by by 50%, it means you're trading half the number of contracts
claims.claim: Large funds cut vol targets to scale: halving vol halves contracts, reducing impact and slippage.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: That is because these allocators are usually paid career risk.
claims.claim: Institutional allocators avoid higher-vol funds because of career risk, so hedge funds lowered vol for those tickets.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: the fees had have not come down commenurate with the reduction in volatility
claims.claim: Fees did not fall in line with lower vol; multistrategy fees have risen, and some funds sit in single-digit returns.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: I actually think fees have really come under pressure.
claims.claim: Flat fees and ETF replicators below 1% show fee pressure in CTAs.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: institutions today are really just optimizing for some kind of average return
claims.claim: Institutions optimize for average returns rather than long compounding, de-emphasizing true risk mitigators like trend.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
claims.quote: they're just highly correlated uh during crisis to uh to the underlying that they're trying to diversify away from.
claims.claim: Strategies that look safe standalone are highly correlated in crises with the assets they diversify.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: the asset the AUM based management fee is so much more valuable relative to the performance fee
claims.claim: With lower vol, AUM-based management fees dominate and push managers into asset gathering with weaker alignment.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: and beta is different than a strategy being commoditized.
claims.claim: Trend following may be commoditized because rules are known, but its return stream is not beta.

claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
claims.quote: we should not be driven by asset gathering dynamics where we're compensated based on management fees
claims.claim: The firm has no asset-based management fee, so performance fee aligns it with investors.
